summary: For ages 12–13: how environmental change (climate change, habitat loss, pollution) shifts where species live, covering three linked mechanisms — range shift, local extinction, and invasive species — unified by differential vulnerability. The core insight is that distribution change is a MOVING band of suitable conditions that populations track (most often poleward and uphill under warming), not animals consciously choosing to migrate; a species that depends on tracking the band persists only if it can follow AND has somewhere suitable left to go. Learners should argue from mechanism and real data, not just apply labels, and explain why specialists, poor dispersers, and montane/polar endemics are most at risk while generalists usually cope better.
misconceptions: Thinking individual animals consciously decide to migrate to a better climate, rather than populations shifting as suitable habitat moves and unsuited individuals fail.
Believing a species that shifts its range is 'fine' — missing that trailing edges suffer local extinction and mountaintop/polar species can run out of room.
Assuming all species can simply move — ignoring dispersal limits, habitat fragmentation with no corridors, and rooted or slow species.
Thinking 'invasive' just means 'non-native' — missing that the harm comes from outcompeting or preying on residents lacking co-evolved defences.
Believing warming is universally bad or universally good for wildlife, rather than creating winners (generalists moving in) and losers (specialists squeezed out).
Treating climate change, habitat loss and pollution as separate unrelated threats rather than compounding drivers of distribution change.

activities.title: Warming the living map: watch suitable habitat move
steps: Work with a map where a coloured band of 'suitable climate' can be shifted north and upslope as temperature rises (e.g. a slider, successive overlays, or a sequence of printed map frames for 1970, today, and a warmer future).

Predict for each of several species where its range will go as the band moves: a generalist butterfly, a heather-moor or alpine specialist pinned near a summit, and a coastal species pinned against the sea.

Advance the warming and observe what happens to each range: the generalist's range glides north and persists; the mountaintop specialist creeps upslope until the mountain ends and its range contracts to a point and disappears from that site — a local extinction if the species still persists on other mountains or further north, but a total loss if it is a montane endemic with no cooler refuge anywhere; the coastal species is trapped with no room to shift.
State in writing, for each species, WHY it coped, shifted, or was lost, naming the trait (generalist vs specialist, good vs poor disperser, 'nowhere to go').
Repeat for the trailing (southern) edge: explain what happens to the population in the far south as it keeps warming and that area becomes too hot.
activities.insight: Distribution change is a band of suitability on the move; populations persist only where conditions let them breed. A full range shift means a trailing edge is lost as a leading edge is gained (though early on, or where the warm limit lies elsewhere, a range may simply expand for a time), and a species with nowhere suitable to follow to (summit, coast, fragmented habitat with no corridor) dies out at that site — a local extinction if it survives elsewhere, but a total loss for an endemic with no refuge anywhere.

activities.title: Introduce an invader: the same change opens a door
steps: On the same map (or a before/after food-web diagram), introduce a non-native species into disturbed or newly warmed ground and observe its range expanding while residents' ranges shrink.

Write what 'invasive' means precisely — not merely 'non-native', but a non-native species that spreads and harms residents, for example by outcompeting them, preying on them, or spreading disease to them, often because they lack co-evolved defences.

Explain how the invasion is enabled: human transport delivering the species (a way in, not a habitat change), plus environmental change in the NEW area such as warming making new ground suitable or disturbance opening space — and, as a separate factor, add that the invader may also thrive because it has escaped the competitors, predators or diseases that held it in check in its native range.
Connect back to the range-shift activity: articulate how the same change that evicts one species opens the door for another.
activities.insight: Invasive harm comes from effects such as outcompeting, preying on or spreading disease to residents that are often co-evolutionarily naive; human transport delivers the species, environmental change in the new area (warming, disturbance) can enable establishment, and escape from the enemies of its native range is an additional, distinct factor that can help it thrive. Change produces winners and losers, not a uniform good or bad outcome.

activities.title: Argue from evidence: justify each species' fate
steps: Work from real, documented case cards (e.g. comma butterfly and Cetti's warbler moving north; ptarmigan and other montane species running out of upslope room; signal crayfish or grey squirrel as invaders), each paired with range maps or data for an earlier decade versus today.
For a chosen species, state a claim about what has happened to its distribution and support it with BOTH the data shown and the mechanism and traits, not a label alone.
Answer challenge questions such as: why did the ptarmigan disappear here but the comma thrive? Why is a specialist more vulnerable to climate change than a near-ubiquitous generalist?
Optionally run this as a role-play debrief: one learner acts as a field ecologist posing the challenge questions and offering case data while others justify each species' fate.
Attempt the diagnostic prompt: 'As the climate warms, a butterfly that used to live only in the south is now found much further north. Explain what has made the butterfly's range move north.'
activities.insight: Claims about distribution change must be backed by mechanism and empirical data; differential vulnerability (specialist vs generalist, disperser vs sessile, cold/high-altitude endemic with no escape) predicts which species cope and which are squeezed out.

activities.title: Winners and losers: sort species and sequence the change
steps: Categorise species as likely winners or losers under warming, and justify each sort from traits (specialist vs generalist, good vs poor disperser, mountaintop/coastal vs those with room to move north).

Put the stages of a trailing-edge local extinction in order: warming → suitable band shifts north → southern/trailing edge becomes unsuitable → local population declines → local extinction at that edge.
Decide what makes a non-native species invasive versus merely non-native, and give the reason.
activities.insight: Learners can classify species by vulnerability with justification and can order the causal sequence from warming to trailing-edge local extinction, consolidating the mechanisms from the earlier activities.

checkQuestion: As the climate warms, a butterfly that used to live only in the south of the country is now found much further north than before. Explain what has happened to make the butterfly's range move north.
checkAnswer: As temperatures rise, northern areas that were once too cold have become warm enough for the butterfly to survive and breed, so the population spreads and persists there; meanwhile the far south may become too hot. Over generations the range shifts north — the suitable conditions moved, and the population tracked them. It isn't individuals deciding to migrate or changing their bodies.
